messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Security Guard
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 49

He is a 71-year-old North American man who has spent most of his adult life working in security, a job that has taught him to notice exits, watch hands, and keep his back to a wall when he can. He is married and describes his home life as steady and familiar, but since the terrorist attack he survived several years ago, even the most ordinary routines feel altered. He talks about that day in a measured way, as though he is still trying to keep the memory in a box that will not quite stay shut.

At the time of the attack, he is on duty in a public building, moving through the familiar rhythm of his shift. He hears the first sharp sounds and initially thinks they are some kind of malfunction or an argument, something he might manage if he gets there quickly enough. Instead, the situation changes in moments. People begin to run, voices rise, and the air fills with a kind of chaos he says he had never truly imagined in a workplace. He remembers the confusion more than any single dramatic image: the stampede of bodies, the frantic search for cover, the fear in strangers’ faces, and his own effort to stay useful while his body wants to freeze. Even now, when he describes it, he returns to the same point—how quickly an ordinary workday becomes a place where survival replaces procedure.

Afterward, he tries to go back to work. He tells himself that security is what he knows, that he cannot let fear take over a role built around calm authority. But once the attack has happened, his mind begins to replay possibilities and near misses. He starts checking doors more often, scanning crowds before he enters them, and positioning himself so he can see everyone in a room. He becomes especially alert to loud bangs, sirens, or sudden commotion. These sounds do not simply startle him; they seem to drop him back into the attack before he can think his way out. At times, his chest tightens and his breathing shortens so abruptly that he has to stop what he is doing and wait for the feeling to pass.

He also notices that sleep has become unreliable. Some nights he falls asleep easily enough, only to wake later with his mind already racing. Other nights he lies awake, listening to the house settle, scanning the dark for a threat he knows is not there but cannot fully dismiss. When he does sleep, he often dreams of crowded spaces or of being unable to get people out in time. He wakes up tired and irritable, more withdrawn with his wife than he wants to be. He apologizes for snapping at her, then grows quiet and embarrassed, as though the loss of control is harder to admit than the fear itself.

In the months that follow, he begins avoiding places that remind him of the attack. Large gatherings feel intolerable. He goes to the grocery store at off-hours, keeps trips short, and prefers to stand near the entrance when he can. He no longer enjoys the noise and unpredictability of public events, and he has started turning down invitations without much explanation. He says he feels “safer not going,” but the safety is thin, bought at the cost of his world growing smaller. He is aware of this shrinking and does not like it. He misses the part of himself that moved through life without calculating every possible danger.

Over time, his mood has darkened in a way that feels different from simple worry. He is less interested in things he used to enjoy, less likely to linger over coffee with friends, and more likely to sit in silence with the television on but not really watching. He finds himself feeling detached, as if some part of him remains back at the scene of the attack while the rest goes through the motions of daily life. At times he wonders why he survived when others did not, and although he does not speak dramatically about guilt, there is a heaviness in the way he carries the memory.

Even now, as a security guard, he performs his duties carefully and with a sense of responsibility, but the job costs him more effort than it once did. He moves through shifts with constant vigilance, aware of how quickly his attention can lock onto a detail and refuse to let go. At home, he is trying to remain the husband he has always been—reliable, steady, present—while privately managing a body that still reacts as if danger may erupt at any moment.
